description: Two separate decisions about the same feature, made by different people for different reasons and pointing in different directions. The style failure is fusion: merging them into one smooth sentence that is individually citable and collectively false.

events.text: Product decision: we're shipping the one-page checkout to 100% of new signups next Monday. Existing customers stay on the two-step flow for now.

Engineering decision, separate from the rollout: we are NOT porting the saved-cards widget to the one-page flow this quarter. New signups won't have saved cards until Q1. That's a capacity call, not a product one.
To be clear those are two different calls — the rollout is happening Monday regardless, and the saved-cards gap is a known tradeoff we're accepting, not a reason to delay.
Usability round on the one-page flow: 7 of 8 completed without help. The one who struggled was looking for saved cards, which matches Devin's tradeoff.

events.text: Since saved cards won't exist on the one-page flow until Q1, new signups will hit an empty slot there. Can you write the empty-state copy for it before Monday's rollout? It's the last thing blocking the release branch.

ground_truth.notes: FUSION is the failure, and it is the one the prompts guard against with 'one claim per line' / 'never combine two claims'. The two decisions here have different owners (Marisol / Devin), different kinds (product / capacity), and no causal relationship — Marisol says so explicitly in the third message, which exists purely so the ground truth is unambiguous. Every stored anti-pattern is composed of true fragments and asserts a false relationship between them: the first invents causality running backwards in time (the usability round is the DAY AFTER the deferral, so it cannot be its cause); the second attributes both calls to 'the team', erasing that one was a capacity constraint someone owns; the third is the tempting one — a terse, well-cited, correctly-ordered summary that still fuses two decisions into one clause and drops who made which. A correct briefing keeps them as separate statements. Fusion scores perfectly on citation accuracy because each fragment traces to a real artifact, which is exactly why a lexical grounding check (F-4) will not catch it either.
